item.title: HTTPS and certificates
item.description: Covers how HTTPS protects communication, how certificates are verified, the kinds of certificates, and why browsers show certificate warnings.
item.content:encoded:
The previous post looked at how a domain is turned into an IP through DNS. But connecting to the IP that DNS returned doesn’t tell you whether that server really belongs to the domain, or whether someone in between is reading the traffic. This post looks at how HTTPS solves this problem, and what the certificate at its center is and how it is verified.

HTTP and HTTPS

HTTP sends requests and responses as plain text, without encryption. Between the browser and the server there are many devices, such as routers and the internet provider’s equipment, as well as other devices on the same Wi-Fi. Anyone on this path can see HTTP requests.

Risk What happens
Eavesdropping Login passwords, cookies and request contents are read in transit
Tampering Another script is inserted into the response, or its contents are changed
Impersonation A fake server responds as if it were the real server

HTTPS sends HTTP wrapped in TLS. As covered in network layers, TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol that encrypts data and uses a certificate to check that the server you connected to is the real one. It addresses each of the three risks above.

What TLS does Risk it prevents
Encryption Eavesdropping. Devices in between see only the IP and port, and can’t read the request path or contents
Integrity check Tampering. Data changed in transit is treated as an error by the receiver
Server authentication Impersonation. The certificate is used to check that the server you connected to owns the domain

The default port for HTTPS is 443, and addresses start with https://. TLS was previously called SSL, so ssl still appears in many configuration entries and tool names.

Public and private keys

Understanding certificates starts with the two kinds of keys TLS uses. The two keys are created as a pair, and what one key does is checked with the other.

Key Held by What it does
Private key Only the server Signs data. A signature is a mark meaning “the owner of this private key produced this data”
Public key Anyone; it is published Checks whether a signature made with the private key is valid

A signature can be checked only with the matching public key, and the private key can’t be derived from the public key. So when the server sends data signed with its private key, the receiver checks it with the public key and knows that the data came from the server holding the private key.

If the private key leaks, someone else can pose as that server. The server’s private key file has restricted permissions and is not put into repositories or images.

Certificates

A public key alone doesn’t tell you whose public key it is. A fake server can also send its own public key and claim it is the public key of app.example.com. So a file in which a trusted organization has confirmed and signed “this public key belongs to this domain” is sent along with it. This file is a certificate, and the organization that signs it is a certificate authority (CA).

Field Content Example
Subject The owner of the certificate CN=app.example.com
Subject Alternative Name (SAN) The list of names this certificate can be used to connect with app.example.com, www.example.com
Issuer The certificate authority that signed it CN=R11, O=Let's Encrypt
Validity period Start and expiry dates 2026-10-01 ~ 2026-12-30
Public key The pair of the server’s private key
Signature The issuer’s signature over all of the above

The browser checks whether the domain it connected to is in the SAN (Subject Alternative Name). The subject’s CN was once used for name checks, but browsers now look only at the SAN. The SAN can also hold a wildcard such as *.example.com, and this name matches subdomains one level down, such as api.example.com. It does not match example.com itself or a.b.example.com.

Certificate authorities and the certificate chain

Certificate authorities are usually split into two levels.

Type What it does Where it is kept
Root CA Signs the certificates of intermediate CAs The root certificate is included in the OS and browser trust store from the start
Intermediate CA Signs server certificates The server sends it along with its own certificate

A trust store is a list that says “certificates that lead to these root certificates are trusted”. Windows, macOS, Linux, Firefox and Java each have their own list.

The line of signatures from the server certificate through the intermediate certificate up to the root certificate is called the certificate chain. The chain is complete only when the server sends both its own certificate and the intermediate certificate. This is why Nginx uses a file with the two certificates joined together (fullchain), and the setup is covered in the Nginx post.

Certificate verification

When the browser receives the server certificate, it checks the items below. If any one of them fails, it stops the connection and shows a warning.

Check What is checked
Chain Whether following the signatures reaches a root certificate in the trust store
Name Whether the domain or IP in the address bar is in the SAN
Validity period Whether the current time is between the start and expiry dates
Private key Whether the server holds the private key that pairs with the certificate’s public key. This is checked in the handshake below

TLS handshake

Before sending an HTTP request, the browser and the server first go through a process that checks the certificate and decides the keys used for encryption. This process is called the TLS handshake. In short, for TLS 1.3, the order is as follows.

  1. The browser sends the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, values for key exchange, and the domain name it wants to connect to. This domain name is called SNI (Server Name Indication).
  2. The server sends the certificate and chain that match the SNI domain, and its values for key exchange. It also signs the handshake messages exchanged so far with its private key and sends the signature.
  3. The browser checks the items from “Certificate verification” above, and checks the signature with the certificate’s public key. If the signature is valid, the other side is the server holding that certificate’s private key.
  4. The browser and the server each calculate the same session key from the key exchange values exchanged in steps 1 and 2. The session key itself is not sent over the network.
  5. After that, HTTP requests and responses are encrypted with the session key and exchanged.

The session key is used for symmetric encryption, which encrypts and decrypts with the same single key. Public key cryptography takes a lot of computation, so it is used only for checking the server and exchanging keys, and the actual data is handled with symmetric encryption.

Because of SNI, the server can choose a different certificate for each domain even when several domains share one IP. Nginx compares the SNI domain with server_name and sends the certificate of that server.

Certificate types

Certificates fall into three types depending on who signed them. The difference is which trust store holds the root certificate used to check that signature.

Type Signed by Trusted by Used for
Public certificate A public certificate authority (Let’s Encrypt, DigiCert, Sectigo and others) Every OS and browser. The root certificates are included from the start Services open to the internet
Private CA certificate A certificate authority the company or team created itself Only PCs and servers where that private CA’s root certificate is installed Internal network servers, development servers
Self-signed certificate The certificate itself Only PCs where that certificate is installed directly. Without it, the warning has to be bypassed on every connection Development environments with few servers, testing

All three types use the same encryption. What differs is whether the browser can check the server, and if it can’t, a warning appears.

Issuing a public certificate

Before issuing a certificate, a public certificate authority checks that the applicant manages the domain. Let’s Encrypt, a free certificate authority, handles this check and the issuance with an automated issuance protocol called ACME.

Challenge What it does Requirement
HTTP-01 You place a value given by the certificate authority at the path http://domain/.well-known/acme-challenge/, and the certificate authority connects to that address to check it The domain must be reachable on port 80 from the internet
DNS-01 You register a value given by the certificate authority as a TXT record for the domain, and the certificate authority checks it through DNS You must be able to edit the DNS records. The server doesn’t need to be open to the internet. Wildcard certificates can be obtained only this way

Let’s Encrypt certificates are valid for 90 days, so automatic renewal is set up along with them. Tools that use ACME include Certbot and acme.sh, and web servers such as Caddy handle issuance and renewal themselves. Paid certificates with longer validity periods also exist, but the maximum validity period of public certificates is getting shorter, so either way a renewal procedure needs to be in place.

Issuing certificates with a private CA

Internal network servers often can’t get a public certificate, because they can’t be reached from the internet or have no public domain. In this case, you create a private CA, issue certificates with it, and install its root certificate on the PCs that will use them. Below is the order for creating one with openssl.

File Content Where it goes
ca.key The private CA’s private key Kept separately in a secure place
ca.crt The private CA’s root certificate The trust store of the PCs and servers that connect
server.key, server.crt The server’s private key and certificate Web server configuration (Nginx’s ssl_certificate_key, ssl_certificate)
server.csr Certificate signing request. Not used after signing

A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is a file that holds the server’s public key and name and asks a certificate authority to sign it. The same format is used when obtaining a public certificate.

How to install ca.crt in the trust store differs by OS.

Environment How to install
Windows certutil -addstore -f Root ca.crt with administrator rights, or open the certificate file and install it in “Trusted Root Certification Authorities”
macOS sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain ca.crt
Ubuntu, Debian Copy ca.crt to /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/, then sudo update-ca-certificates
Firefox Uses its own trust store, so import it separately in the certificate manager in settings
Java applications Add it to the JDK’s trust store with keytool -importcert

Whoever has ca.key can create a certificate for any domain, and PCs with ca.crt installed trust all of those certificates. So ca.key is managed more strictly than a server certificate’s private key. The details are in Risk on PCs with a root certificate installed.

Generating a self-signed certificate

A self-signed certificate is created together with its private key in a single command, without a CA. The certificate is signed with its own private key, so the receiver has no root certificate to check it against. As a result, a warning appears on PCs where that certificate hasn’t been installed directly.

basicConstraints on the last line is the field that sets whether this certificate is a CA that can sign other certificates. openssl req -x509 adds CA extensions in its default configuration, so without this field the certificate is created with CA:TRUE. The step 1 command that created the private CA’s root certificate also gets CA:TRUE for the same reason. The reason for specifying CA:FALSE is in Risk on PCs with a root certificate installed.

Self-signed certificates and private CAs compared

With both approaches, the server holds the same two files: a private key and a certificate. A private CA adds the CA’s private key and root certificate. The root certificate is installed on the connecting side, and the CA’s private key is not placed on the server.

File Self-signed Private CA
server.key (the server’s private key) Server Server
server.crt (the server’s certificate, including the public key) Server Server
ca.crt (root certificate) None The trust store of the connecting PCs and servers
ca.key (the CA’s private key) None Kept separately somewhere other than the servers and PCs, and used only when issuing certificates

To connect without a warning, a certificate has to be added to the trust store of each connecting PC. Which certificate is added, and when it has to be added again, differs between the two approaches.

Task Self-signed Private CA
Connecting without a warning Install the server certificate as a trusted certificate on each PC Install the root certificate once on each PC
Adding a server Install the new server’s certificate again on each PC Only sign with the same CA; nothing is installed again on the PCs
Renewing a certificate Install the changed certificate again on each PC. Browsers that were bypassing the warning have to bypass it again Nothing is installed again on the PCs
Creating a certificate One command Three steps: creating the CA, creating the CSR, signing

For example, with 3 servers and 10 connecting PCs, self-signed certificates mean installing 3 server certificates on each PC, 30 installations in total. A private CA means installing 1 root certificate on each PC, 10 installations, and nothing is installed again on the PCs when servers are added or certificates are renewed.

When nothing is installed on the PCs and the warning is bypassed, both approaches show the ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID warning, so users see no difference. The difference grows as servers and users increase and connections need to work without a warning.

A certificate used on only one development PC can also be created with the mkcert tool. mkcert -install creates a private CA on that PC and adds it to the trust store, and mkcert localhost 192.168.0.20 creates a certificate signed by that CA. Since it is the private CA approach, no warning appears on that PC, and a warning appears on other PCs where the root certificate isn’t installed.

Risk on PCs with a root certificate installed

A root certificate added to the trust store has, by default, no limit on the domains it can sign for. So if the CA’s private key leaks, the problems follow in this order.

  1. Whoever has the private key can create a certificate for any domain, such as bank.example.com.
  2. PCs with the root certificate installed trust that certificate as a valid certificate.
  3. If the attacker is on the same network or can change DNS responses, they can read and change HTTPS traffic between that PC and the real server without a warning. This is called a man-in-the-middle attack.

If a server is compromised, what leaks is the server’s private key and certificate. The server certificate is not a CA and can’t sign other certificates, so the attacker can only impersonate the names in that certificate’s SAN. This limit holds as long as ca.key is not kept on the server as well.

The same problem can occur with self-signed certificates. If a self-signed certificate with CA:TRUE is installed in the trust store, that certificate is placed in the same position as a root certificate. Its private key is on the server, so if the server is compromised, steps 1 to 3 above can happen as they are. This is why the command above specifies CA:FALSE, and a certificate with CA:FALSE, even when installed, is trusted only for the names in its SAN.

Task Method
Storing ca.key Don’t upload it to servers; keep it separately in a place used only for issuing certificates
Limiting signing scope Add the Name Constraints extension to the root certificate to limit signing to internal domains such as .test. Support for this extension differs by OS and browser
Installation scope Install the root certificate only on the PCs that need it, and remove it from the trust store when it is no longer used
Self-signed certificates Create them with basicConstraints=critical,CA:FALSE

Certificates for IP addresses

When connecting by IP, as in https://192.168.0.20, the browser checks whether that IP is in the SAN as IP:192.168.0.20. Connecting by IP with a certificate that holds only a domain gives a name mismatch and a warning.

Private IPs are used as the same addresses on many internal networks, so public certificate authorities don’t issue certificates for private IPs. If an internal network server has to be reached by IP, issue the certificate with the IP in the SAN, as in step 3 of Issuing certificates with a private CA. If a name can be given through internal DNS or the hosts file, the certificate can also be issued for a domain.

Certificate warnings

When certificate verification fails, the browser shows a warning screen instead of the page. The error code on the warning screen tells you which check failed. Below are Chrome’s codes.

Error code Failed check Common causes
NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID Chain A PC without the self-signed certificate or the private CA’s root certificate installed, the server not sending the intermediate certificate
NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID Name The domain or IP connected to is not in the SAN
NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID Validity period Expired certificate, the PC’s clock is wrong

Clicking the site information icon in the address bar shows the certificate’s issuer, SAN and validity period.

Connections that bypass the warning

Continuing from “Advanced” on the warning screen opens the page. This choice stays in that browser as an exception for a period of time, but it doesn’t mean the certificate is now trusted. So problems remain in the following cases.

Case Result
Another person or another browser connects Each person has to bypass the warning again
fetch requests and WebSocket (wss://) connections the page sends to another address (an API server and so on) The warning screen appears only for pages opened from the address bar, so connections to that address, which has no exception registered, fail without a warning
Another server or app makes the call A server’s HTTP client makes no exceptions, so it fails with a certificate error

For a server used by many people, instead of bypassing the warning, use a public certificate or install the private CA’s root certificate on the PCs that use it, so the warning doesn’t appear at all.

HSTS

HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) is a response header with which the server tells the browser “connect to this domain only over HTTPS from now on”.

Part Meaning
max-age How long the browser remembers this instruction, in seconds. 31536000 is one year
includeSubDomains Applies the same to subdomains

A browser that has received this header handles two things differently for the max-age period.

  • Even if http:// is typed in the address bar, it changes it to https:// before sending the request. This prevents attacks that intercept HTTP requests in transit.
  • It removes the button for continuing on that domain’s certificate warning screen.

Because of the second behavior, HSTS is not turned on for servers that use a self-signed certificate or private CA certificate not installed on the connecting PCs. Turning it on makes that domain unreachable. HSTS remembered by the browser stays until max-age passes, even if the header is removed. Nginx’s HTTPS setup and HTTP→HTTPS redirection are in the Nginx post.

Certificate check commands

Outside the browser, use openssl and curl to check the certificate the server sends.

-servername is the domain sent as SNI. A server with several domains on one IP sends a different certificate depending on this value.

curl -k skips certificate verification. It is used only to see whether the server responds, not as a way to fix a certificate problem.

Command summary

Task Command
Check a server’s certificate openssl s_client -connect domain:443 -servername domain
View a certificate file’s contents openssl x509 -in file -noout -text
Create a private CA openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt -days 3650
Create a self-signed certificate openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout server.key -out server.crt -addext "basicConstraints=critical,CA:FALSE"
Create a server private key and CSR openssl req -new -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout server.key -out server.csr
Sign with the private CA openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out server.crt -extfile san.ext
Install a root certificate (Ubuntu) Copy to /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/, then sudo update-ca-certificates
Request with verification by the private CA curl --cacert ca.crt https://domain

item.title: DNS and domains
item.description: Covers how DNS turns a domain into an IP, the records it uses, the hosts file and internal DNS, and the commands for checking lookup results.
item.content:encoded:
The previous posts connected by IP, as in 192.168.0.20. In practice you often connect with a domain such as example.com, and the browser turns the domain into an IP before connecting. This post looks at that process, DNS, along with records, the hosts file, internal DNS and how to check lookup results. In terms of the network layers, DNS is an application layer protocol and uses UDP port 53 (TCP port 53 when the response is large).

Domains and DNS

A domain is a name given to an IP address so that people can remember it. DNS (Domain Name System) is the system that turns a domain into an IP address.

When you type https://api.example.com into the browser, the browser first asks DNS for the IP of api.example.com, then connects to the IP it gets back (203.0.113.20). If the server moves to a different IP, only the value in DNS needs to change, and users keep connecting with the same domain.

Domain structure

A domain is split by dots, and the further right a part is, the wider its scope.

Part Name Who decides it
.com Top-level domain (TLD) Set by international bodies. .com, .org, .kr and so on
example Registered domain Bought and registered through a domain registrar
api Subdomain Created by the domain owner by adding a record in DNS

Once example.com is registered, names under it such as api.example.com, www.example.com and dev.example.com can be created without registering them separately.

Subdomains and paths

A subdomain is a name placed in front of the domain, and a part after the domain such as /users/12 is the path. The two are handled in different places.

Part In https://api.example.com/users/12 Handled by
Subdomain and domain api.example.com DNS turns it into an IP. Each subdomain can be sent to a different IP
Path /users/12 DNS does not look at the path. The server at that IP (Nginx, the backend) receives it and routes it

So the addresses that separate the frontend and backend can also be built in two ways.

Approach Addresses Characteristics
Split by path example.com, example.com/api The approach in the Nginx post. There is one address, so no CORS setup is needed
Split by subdomain example.com, api.example.com DNS can send each to a different server. The hosts differ, so the origins differ, and the backend needs a CORS setup

Records

Each line written in DNS for a domain is called a record. Records are stored on the name servers covered below.

From the left: the name, the TTL (how long this result may be kept in a cache, in seconds), the record type, and the value. TTL is covered below in “Caching and TTL”.

Type Value Used for
A IPv4 address Pointing a domain at an IP
AAAA IPv6 address Pointing a domain at an IPv6 address
CNAME Another domain An alias. In the example above, www.example.com follows the IP of example.com
MX Mail server domain The server that receives mail sent to this domain
TXT Text Domain ownership verification, mail sender authentication
NS Name server domain The authoritative name server responsible for this domain

CNAME

An A record returns an IP directly, and a CNAME record returns another domain name.

Record Name looked up Value returned
A example.com 203.0.113.10 (an IP)
CNAME www.example.com example.com (another domain)

So finding the IP of www.example.com takes two lookups.

  1. Looking up www.example.com returns example.com as a CNAME instead of an IP. This means www.example.com is another name for example.com.
  2. Next, example.com is looked up and the A record’s 203.0.113.10 comes back.
  3. The browser connects to 203.0.113.10, the last value it received.

DNS carries out the second lookup itself, so the browser receives only one IP.

CNAME is used so that the IP is managed in only one place. Take the case where the server IP changes from 203.0.113.10 to 203.0.113.50.

How the www record is set Records to change when the IP changes
The IP written directly with an A record Two: example.com and www.example.com
Linked to example.com with a CNAME One: example.com. www.example.com changes along with it

When a cloud deployment service tells you to “point blog.example.com at myapp.host.example with a CNAME”, it is the same principle. The service company manages the A record of myapp.host.example, so even if the service’s IP changes, the record in your DNS stays as it is.

Name servers

A name server is a DNS server that holds a domain’s records and answers the question “what is the IP of this domain”.

No single server holds the information for every domain on the internet. Like the domain structure, it is split into levels: each name server knows only its own range and hands the levels below to the next name server. This is called delegation.

Name server What it knows
Root name server The addresses of the name servers responsible for each top-level domain (.com, .kr and so on)
TLD name server (.com) The addresses of the name servers responsible for each domain under .com (example.com and so on)
Authoritative name server (example.com) The actual records of example.com and its subdomains

“Authoritative” means the server holds that domain’s records itself, so it can answer without asking anywhere else.

Domain registration and name servers

When you register a domain, you specify the authoritative name servers for it. You can use the name servers the registrar provides by default, or switch to the name servers of a DNS service such as Cloudflare or AWS Route 53. The specified name servers are registered with the TLD name server as NS records.

After that, records such as A and CNAME are added and changed in the admin page of the specified name servers. Two or more name servers are specified so that if one stops, the other can still answer lookups.

Resolvers and name servers

Besides name servers, which answer, DNS servers also include resolvers, which go around asking.

Resolver Authoritative name server
What it does Asks several name servers in turn on behalf of your PC to find the final IP, and keeps the result in a cache Answers with the records of the domains it is responsible for
Examples Your internet provider’s DNS, 8.8.8.8 (Google), 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare), a company’s internal DNS The name servers of the DNS service specified for the domain
The “DNS server” field in a PC’s network settings What goes here is a resolver Not entered here

Lookup process

The first lookup of api.example.com goes like this.

  1. Your PC checks the hosts file and its own cache. If the name is there, the lookup ends here.
  2. If not, it asks the resolver set in the network settings.
  3. The resolver asks a root name server and gets the address of the TLD name server responsible for .com.
  4. The resolver asks the TLD name server and gets the address of the authoritative name server for example.com.
  5. The resolver asks the authoritative name server and gets 203.0.113.20, the IP of api.example.com.
  6. The resolver stores the result in its cache and returns it to your PC.

Caching and TTL

A DNS response carries a TTL (Time To Live, how long it stays valid). Resolvers and PCs keep the result in a cache for the TTL, and when the same domain is asked again, they answer directly without steps 3 to 5.

So when you change the IP in a record, the change does not reach every user right away. Resolvers and PCs that cached the previous value keep connecting to the old IP until the TTL runs out. Shortening the TTL before moving a server makes the changed value take effect sooner.

The hosts file

During development and testing, there are times when you need to connect by domain name but can’t create a record in DNS, or shouldn’t create one yet. The hosts file is used in these cases.

The hosts file is a file on the PC where pairs of domains and IPs are written directly. As in step 1 of the lookup process above, the PC reads this file before asking the resolver. A name written here goes straight to the written IP without a DNS lookup.

OS Location
Windows C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts (edit with administrator rights)
Linux, mac /etc/hosts

Write one IP and domain per line.

Uses of the hosts file

Situation Why connecting by IP doesn’t work What to write
Splitting several services on one server by name Nginx uses server_name to look at the domain name in the request and pick a server block. Connecting by IP gives no name to decide which service to send it to As in the first and second lines of the example above, a different name for each service on the same IP
Checking an HTTPS certificate Certificates are issued for domain names. Connecting by IP doesn’t match the name on the certificate, so the browser shows a warning The domain on the certificate and the development server’s IP
Checking a new server before moving to it Changing the DNS record sends every user to the new server, and if something goes wrong, it is hard to go back to the old value during the TTL As in the third line of the example above, the production domain and the new server’s IP. Only your PC goes to the new server
Naming servers in a team without the “Internal DNS” below IPs are hard to remember, and when a server’s IP changes, every setting that has that IP written in it has to be changed A name for each server, as in 192.168.0.30 db.example.test

The hosts file applies before DNS, so if you don’t remove the entry after checking, only your PC keeps connecting to that IP. If “it works for others but only my PC goes to the old server”, check the hosts file first.

.test is a top-level domain reserved for testing, so it doesn’t overlap with real domains on the internet.

Resolver settings

“The resolver set in the network settings” from step 2 of the lookup process is set separately on each PC and server. If this value is empty, communication by IP works but every domain lookup fails.

Available resolvers

Type Example Characteristics
Router 192.168.0.1 Many routers also act as a resolver and pass the questions they receive on to the provider’s DNS
Company internal DNS An internal IP set by the company Answers for internal names, covered in “Internal DNS” below, as well as internet domains
Provider DNS The address given by the internet provider Often received automatically when connecting to the internet
Public DNS 8.8.8.8 (Google), 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare) Usable from any network. It doesn’t know internal names, and on company networks that block external DNS it doesn’t respond

Usually two or more resolvers are listed. If the first resolver doesn’t respond, the lookup continues with the second.

nameserver in configuration files

In configuration files, resolvers are often written under the name nameserver. Linux and many tools have traditionally called “the DNS server to ask” by this name. A nameserver in a configuration file is not an authoritative name server from the “Name servers” section above, but the resolver this PC or server asks.

Where it is written Example value Meaning
nameserver in the server’s /etc/resolv.conf, nameservers in netplan 8.8.8.8 The resolver this server asks
The domain’s NS record ns1.dns-provider.example. The authoritative name server that holds this domain’s records

Resolvers on Linux servers

On Linux servers such as Ubuntu, a program running inside the server called systemd-resolved acts as the resolver. Programs on the server ask it, and systemd-resolved in turn asks a resolver outside the server, such as the router or 8.8.8.8 from the table above. Below, this resolver is called the upstream resolver to tell it apart from systemd-resolved inside the server.

systemd-resolved doesn’t decide the upstream resolver’s address itself; it receives it through the network settings. netplan and the renderer are involved in these settings.

Name What it does
netplan On Ubuntu, the YAML files (/etc/netplan/*.yaml) where network settings such as the IP, gateway and resolvers are written, and the tool that hands those files to the renderer. It does not configure the network card itself
Renderer The program that takes netplan’s settings, actually assigns the IP and gateway to the network card, and passes the resolver list to systemd-resolved. It is set with the renderer: entry in the netplan file

There are two renderers, and they do the same job.

Renderer Default on Characteristics
networkd (systemd-networkd) Ubuntu Server Only reads and applies configuration files. Suits servers whose settings rarely change
NetworkManager Ubuntu Desktop Has features for changing connections often, such as choosing Wi-Fi, connecting to a VPN, the network menu on screen and the nmcli command

The two renderers use different configuration formats. netplan lets you write one YAML format and converts it into the format of the chosen renderer, so the user doesn’t need to know the difference. Whichever renderer is used, systemd-resolved still acts as the resolver.

The settings are passed along in this order.

Order Where What it does
1 netplan configuration file The upstream resolvers are written under nameservers
2 netplan apply Converts the file into the renderer’s configuration format and hands it over
3 Renderer (networkd or NetworkManager) Applies the settings to the network card and passes the upstream resolver list to systemd-resolved
4 systemd-resolved Forwards lookups using the upstream resolver list it received
5 /etc/resolv.conf Contains nameserver 127.0.0.53. 127.0.0.53 points to systemd-resolved inside the server itself, and programs on the server ask this address
Entry Meaning When empty
renderer The renderer that applies the settings The default, networkd, is used
addresses (top level) This server’s IP. /24 means addresses whose first three parts, 192.168.0, are the same are treated as the same range The server doesn’t connect to the network
to: default and via under routes The two lines are one rule. to: default means every other destination with no route of its own (the internet and other ranges), and via is the gateway those packets are handed to (the address of a router in the same range). The example means “hand every packet for other destinations to 192.168.0.1” Packets can’t leave the same range, so the internet can’t be reached even by IP
addresses under nameservers The resolvers to ask about domains Communication by IP works, and only domain lookups fail

The same 192.168.0.1 appears in both via and nameservers in the example because one router acts as both the gateway and the resolver.

Even if resolvers are written in the configuration file, the list in systemd-resolved is empty if the settings haven’t been applied. Check the values actually in use with resolvectl status.

If this command prints nothing, systemd-resolved has nowhere to forward questions to, and every domain lookup fails. Check nameservers in the configuration file, apply it again with sudo netplan apply, then use the same command to see whether the list is filled in. netplan apply reapplies the network, so the SSH connection may drop briefly.

If the list is still empty after reapplying, the renderer that received the settings is different from the renderer that actually manages the network card. For example, if netplan hands the settings over with renderer: networkd but NetworkManager manages the card, the resolver list networkd received isn’t applied to that card. In nmcli device status, a card shown as connected is managed by NetworkManager, and one shown as unmanaged is managed by networkd. Servers without NetworkManager installed don’t have this command, and networkd manages the card. Write the resolver settings on the side of the renderer that actually manages the card.

The settings above apply to servers where a person writes a static IP by hand, such as servers you install yourself. Servers created in the cloud receive their IP and resolvers automatically, so netplan usually isn’t edited by hand.

Item Self-installed server Cloud server (AWS, GCP, Azure and so on)
IP, gateway, resolvers Written by a person during installation Received at boot through DHCP (a way of automatically handing out an IP, gateway and resolvers to devices connected to a network)
netplan file Created by the installer or written by a person Created by cloud-init (a program that sets up the network, accounts and SSH keys when a cloud server first boots)
Where to change resolvers The netplan file The network (VPC) settings in the cloud console. Files created by cloud-init can be regenerated, so changes made by hand may be lost

Either way, checking resolvers with resolvectl status works the same, and so does the container resolver behavior covered below in “Name lookup on Docker networks”.

On a Windows PC, check the resolvers in use under the “DNS Servers” entry of ipconfig /all.

Internal DNS

Companies sometimes run a DNS server used only inside the internal network. Internal DNS holds the names of internal servers, as in db.corp.example.test → 192.168.0.30, and these names can’t be looked up from the internet.

Situation Internal name lookup
Office internal network Works. The network settings use the internal DNS as the resolver
Connected through a VPN from home Works if the VPN sets the internal DNS as the resolver
From home without a VPN Doesn’t work. Resolvers on the internet don’t know internal names

If you’re connected to the VPN and IPs work but internal names don’t, the VPN hasn’t passed on its DNS settings. Check the DNS server entry of the VPN adapter in ipconfig /all.

Name lookup on Docker networks

IP addresses and ports said containers on the same Docker network can connect to each other by name, as in api:8000. This is DNS too. Docker runs a built-in DNS server (127.0.0.11) for each user-created network and answers container names with that container’s IP.

The default bridge network has no such name lookup, so containers can be reached by name only on networks created with docker network create.

Internet domains, as opposed to container names, follow the server’s resolver settings. A container can’t reach the server’s 127.0.0.53, so Docker takes the upstream resolver list that systemd-resolved uses, from “Resolvers on Linux servers” above, and uses it.

Server’s resolver settings Resolvers the container uses
systemd-resolved has upstream resolvers Those resolvers
No upstream resolvers Docker’s defaults, 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4

So if the server’s resolver settings are empty, docker pull can’t look up the image registry’s domain, and build steps such as RUN apt-get ask 8.8.8.8. On company networks that block external DNS, these steps fail too. In this case, fill in the server’s resolver settings first, and if a container needs a specific resolver, use docker run --dns 192.168.0.1 or the "dns" entry in the Docker configuration file (/etc/docker/daemon.json).

Checking lookup results

Line Meaning
Server The resolver used for this lookup
Non-authoritative answer The answer came from a resolver, from its cache or a lookup on your behalf, rather than from the authoritative name server
Address The IP that was looked up

Looking up a domain with a CNAME using dig +short prints the CNAME value and then the final IP. This shows the two lookups from “CNAME” above in the result.

nslookup and dig ask the DNS server directly, so they don’t read the hosts file. It is expected that a value written in the hosts file doesn’t show up in nslookup. To see the result with the hosts file applied, check the IP that ping shows.

Clear your PC’s DNS cache with the commands below.

Order for checking domain connection problems

Symptom What to check
DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN in the browser There is no record for that name. Check for typos in the domain and whether the record is registered with nslookup
Connecting by IP works but by domain doesn’t A DNS problem. Check whether the nslookup result is that IP
Every domain lookup fails on a server (docker pull fails, Temporary failure in name resolution) If ping 8.8.8.8 works and dig domain @8.8.8.8 also works, the internet connection is fine and the server’s resolver settings are missing. Check the DNS server list in resolvectl status
The record was changed but connections still go to the old server Caching during the TTL. Check whether the new value is in effect with dig @8.8.8.8, and clear your PC’s cache
Only your PC goes to a different server Check whether that domain is written in the hosts file
Internal names don’t work after connecting to the VPN Check the DNS server settings of the VPN adapter

Command summary

Task Command
Look up a domain’s IP nslookup domain, dig +short domain
Look up through a specific resolver dig domain @8.8.8.8
Look up a specific record type dig domain CNAME, nslookup -type=MX domain
Check the resolvers in use ipconfig /all (Windows), resolvectl status (Linux)
Edit the hosts file Windows C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts, Linux and mac /etc/hosts
Clear the DNS cache ipconfig /flushdns (Windows), resolvectl flush-caches (Linux)
Look up a name inside a container docker exec container getent hosts name

item.title: VPN
item.description: Covers how a VPN lets people from outside into an internal network, and how it differs from port forwarding and SSH tunnels.
item.content:encoded:
Port forwarding in the previous post opens an internal server’s port to the internet, so anyone who knows the address can try to connect. If the people who need the internal server from outside are a known group, you can let only those people into the internal network instead of opening a port. This post looks at how that method, the VPN, works, and how it differs from port forwarding and SSH tunnels.

The examples use these addresses.

Name Address
Public IP of the home router 198.51.100.50
Public IP of the company VPN server 203.0.113.10
Internal company server 192.168.0.20
IP the VPN server gives my PC 10.8.0.5

VPN

A VPN (Virtual Private Network) builds an encrypted path on top of a connection that crosses the internet, making a distant PC act as if it were inside the internal network.

Connecting to a VPN does two things.

What happens Result
An encrypted path is created between my PC and the company VPN server On the internet segment in between, the contents can’t be read or altered
The VPN server gives my PC an IP used inside the network (10.8.0.5) To the internal company servers, my PC is a computer on the internal network

So even from home, you can connect to an internal company server by its private IP, as in ssh dev@192.168.0.20. The internal server’s port is not open to the internet.

Tunnels

The encrypted path is called a tunnel. A tunnel works by doing the encapsulation seen in network layers one more time.

A request my PC sends to the internal server becomes two layers like this.

Layer Source Destination Contents
Inner packet 10.8.0.5 192.168.0.20:22 The request originally being sent. It is encrypted as a whole
Outer packet 198.51.100.50 203.0.113.10 The outer envelope for crossing the internet. It carries the inner packet
  1. The VPN program on my PC encrypts the inner packet, puts it in an outer packet, and sends it to the company VPN server’s public IP.
  2. Routers on the internet forward it by looking only at the outer packet’s addresses. The inner contents are encrypted and can’t be read.
  3. The VPN server removes the outer packet, decrypts the inner packet, and sends it to 192.168.0.20 on the internal network.
  4. The response comes back the same way in reverse.

The internal server sees the request as coming from 10.8.0.5. My home public IP is visible only as far as the VPN server.

Comparison with port forwarding

These are two methods for the same goal: letting people reach an internal server from outside.

Port forwarding VPN
How it works Opens one port of the internal server to the internet Makes an outside PC act as if it were inside the internal network
Who can try to connect Anyone who knows the public IP and port Only people with a VPN account
What can be reached The one port that was opened The internal network the VPN allows
Ports opened to the internet One per service One port on the VPN server
Setup Router or firewall rules A VPN server, plus a VPN program and account for each user

Port forwarding fits cases where anyone needs to connect, such as a public web service. If only a known group needs internal admin pages, databases, or SSH, you can have them come in through the VPN and leave each service’s port closed.

Keep in mind that a VPN can open the whole internal network to anyone who connects. The VPN server or firewall can set which internal addresses and ports VPN users can reach.

Company VPNs and personal VPN services

They use the same technology for different purposes.

Company VPN Personal VPN service
Purpose Reaching the company’s internal network from outside Hiding where I connect from, and encrypting the public Wi-Fi segment
End of the tunnel The company VPN server, with the company’s internal network behind it The VPN provider’s server, with the ordinary internet behind it
My IP as seen by websites The company’s public IP (with a full tunnel) The VPN provider server’s IP

With a personal VPN service, the tunnel ends at the VPN provider’s server, and from there traffic goes out to the ordinary internet. So it has no way into an internal network. Also, because the tunnel is unwrapped at the VPN provider’s server, the provider can see anything not encrypted with HTTPS.

Full tunnel and split tunnel

After connecting to a VPN, which traffic goes through the tunnel depends on the VPN settings.

Full tunnel Split tunnel
What goes through the tunnel All traffic Only traffic to internal company addresses (192.168.0.x and so on)
Reaching ordinary websites Goes out through the company Goes out directly through the home internet
Advantage The company firewall and security policies apply to every connection The ordinary internet doesn’t slow down, since it doesn’t pass through the company line
Disadvantage All traffic passes through the company and can slow down Company security policies don’t apply to ordinary internet connections

If even the ordinary internet slows down after connecting to the VPN, it may be a full tunnel. Which one it is can be seen with the route check commands in “Checking the connection” below.

Common protocols

VPNs are divided by the method (protocol) used to build the tunnel.

Protocol Characteristics Default port
OpenVPN Encrypts with TLS. It has been in use for a long time, so many devices and clients support it UDP 1194 (can also be set to TCP 443)
WireGuard Short configuration and code, and fast connections. It is included in the Linux kernel UDP 51820
IPsec A standard that works at the internet layer. Widely used for device-to-device VPNs linking company offices UDP 500, 4500

VPN programs handed out at work (such as a firewall vendor’s client) also build the tunnel internally with one of these or with the vendor’s own method. As a user, you get the connection address, an account, and a certificate or configuration file, and connect with them.

Comparison with SSH tunnels

The SSH tunnel used in Redis GUI tools also creates an encrypted path. The scope is different, though.

This command sends requests made to port 6379 on my PC through the SSH connection to the server, which passes them on to 127.0.0.1:6379. Through one server you can reach over SSH, it connects only the one port you specify.

SSH tunnel VPN
What it connects The one port written in the command The internal network
What you need A server you can reach over SSH, and an account A VPN server and a VPN account
Internal IP my PC gets None Yes (10.8.0.5)
Where it is used Briefly reaching a port such as a database or Redis on one server Ongoing use of several internal servers and services

Checking the connection

After connecting to the VPN, check in this order.

Result Meaning
No VPN adapter or IP The VPN connection itself did not succeed
There is an IP, but the route to internal addresses doesn’t go through the VPN A routing problem. Check the split tunnel address ranges in the VPN settings
The route for all addresses (0.0.0.0) goes through the VPN It is a full tunnel
The route is correct, but the connection fails The VPN server or firewall may be blocking access to that server or port

Overlapping home and company address ranges

If the home router and the company’s internal network both use the 192.168.0.x range, the PC can’t tell whether 192.168.0.20 is an address on the home network or the company’s, even when connected to the VPN. In that case the request goes out to the home network instead of the VPN, and the company server can’t be reached.

If the same range shows up with two routes in route print or ip route, this is the case. Changing the home router’s internal range to one that doesn’t overlap with the company’s, such as 192.168.50.x, resolves it.

Summary

Task How
Let a known group use the internal network from outside VPN
Publish a service anyone can reach Port forwarding
Briefly reach one port on one server SSH tunnel ssh -L localPort:targetAddress:targetPort account@server
Check that the VPN is connected Look for the VPN adapter and IP in ipconfig or ip addr
Check which addresses go through the VPN route print, ip route

item.title: NAT and port forwarding
item.description: Covers how a computer with a private IP reaches the internet (NAT), and how requests from outside are let in to an internal server (port forwarding).
item.content:encoded:
The previous post said a private IP can’t be reached from the internet, because every internal network uses private IPs on its own. Yet an office PC with a private IP still opens websites. This post looks at how a computer with a private IP gets out to the internet (NAT), and how requests from outside are let in to an internal server (port forwarding).

The examples use these addresses.

Name Address
Public IP of the router (or company firewall) 203.0.113.10
Internal PC 192.168.0.31
Internal server 192.168.0.20
External server on the internet 198.51.100.10

NAT

NAT (Network Address Translation) changes the source address of a request to the public IP as it leaves the internal network, and changes it back to the original internal address when the response returns. A router does this at home; a firewall or router does it at a company.

When an internal PC sends a request to an external server, it goes like this.

Step Source Destination What happens
1 192.168.0.31:51000 198.51.100.10:443 The internal PC sends the request
2 203.0.113.10:40001 198.51.100.10:443 The router replaces the source with its public IP and a new port, and records 40001 ↔ 192.168.0.31:51000
3 198.51.100.10:443 203.0.113.10:40001 The external server responds to the router’s public IP
4 198.51.100.10:443 192.168.0.31:51000 The router looks up its record and passes the response to the internal PC

The external server only sees the router’s public IP, never the internal PC’s private IP. This record is also what lets many internal PCs share one public IP: the router records a different port for each PC, so responses go back to the right PC without getting mixed up.

Requests from outside

NAT can only route back responses to requests that were sent from inside first. When a new request arrives from outside at 203.0.113.10:8080, the router has no record for that port. It can’t tell which internal computer to send it to, so the request is dropped.

So to make an internal server reachable from outside, you have to tell the router in advance which internal address requests on which port go to. That is port forwarding.

Port forwarding

Port forwarding is a rule written into a router or firewall saying “requests arriving on this port go to this internal address”.

External port Internal address to send to Purpose
8080 192.168.0.20:8080 The internal server’s web service
2222 192.168.0.20:22 The internal server’s SSH

With this rule, connecting from outside to http://203.0.113.10:8080 makes the router pass the request on to 192.168.0.20:8080. As in the second row, the external and internal ports can differ. From outside you connect with ssh -p 2222 dev@203.0.113.10, and the request goes to port 22 on the internal server.

The rule is set in the router’s admin page at home, and in the firewall settings at a company.

The client IP the server sees

Port forwarding only changes the destination address, not the source. So the internal server sees the public IP of whoever connected, as is.

A reverse proxy like Nginx is different. A reverse proxy receives the request and sends a new one itself, so the backend behind it sees the proxy’s IP instead of the client’s. That is why the backend needs headers like X-Forwarded-For to learn the original client IP.

Port forwarding Reverse proxy
What it does Changes the destination address and passes it on Receives the request and sends it again as a new request
What it looks at (layer) IP address, port (layers 3 and 4) HTTP path, headers (layer 7)
Client IP the server sees The original client’s IP The proxy’s IP
Path and header handling None Can split by path and add headers

Connecting to the public address from inside

After setting up port forwarding, connecting to 203.0.113.10:8080 from a PC on the same internal network may fail. The request has to leave through the router and come back in, and some devices don’t support this (NAT loopback, or hairpin NAT) or have it turned off.

From inside, connect with the private IP, as in 192.168.0.20:8080. Check that port forwarding works from outside the internal network, for example over mobile data.

Docker -p and port forwarding

docker run -p 8080:80 works on the same principle. A container gets a private IP such as 172.17.0.2 on a separate network inside the host. -p is the option that has Docker set up a rule on the host sending requests on the host’s port 8080 to that container’s port 80.

Router port forwarding Docker -p 8080:80
Address used from outside Public IP 203.0.113.10:8080 Host IP 192.168.0.20:8080
Where it is actually received Internal server 192.168.0.20:8080 Container 172.17.0.2:80
Where the rule lives Router or firewall settings Docker adds it to the host’s firewall rules (iptables)

On Linux, the rules Docker adds take effect before firewall settings like ufw. Even if ufw blocks 8080, a port opened with -p 8080:80 can still be reached from outside. For a port meant only for use on the same server, set the bind address with -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80, as in the previous post.

Who can reach a forwarded port

A port opened by port forwarding can be tried by anyone who knows that public IP and port. Public IP ranges are public knowledge, and programs that hunt for open ports are scanning the whole internet all the time. Even if you never share the address, connection attempts arrive soon after the port is opened.

What to check Why
Open only the ports you need Each open port adds one more program that can be attacked
Check that the service requires a login or password An admin page or API with no authentication can be used by anyone who connects
See whether the firewall can restrict which IPs are allowed Connections can be limited to known places, such as the office IP
Check that it is served over HTTPS Over HTTP, what is exchanged is not encrypted

Ports that only the app server needs, such as a database or Redis, are not opened with port forwarding. Even with a password set, they become targets for attacks that keep trying passwords.

If the people who need the internal server from outside are a known group, there is another way: instead of opening a port to the internet, let only those people into the internal network. That is the VPN, covered in the next post.

Summary

Task How
Reach websites from an internal PC NAT. The router handles it automatically
Reach an internal server from outside Add a port forwarding rule to the router or firewall
Reach a container through a host port docker run -p hostPort:containerPort
Keep a container port to the same server -p 127.0.0.1:hostPort:containerPort
Check that port forwarding works Connect to publicIP:port from outside the internal network (mobile data, for example)

item.title: IP addresses and ports
item.description: Covers what the IP and port in a server address each point to, the difference between public and private IPs and between localhost and 0.0.0.0, and what to check when you can't connect.
item.content:encoded:
In an address like http://192.168.0.20:8080, 192.168.0.20 is the IP address and 8080 is the port. In terms of the layers from the previous post, the IP address is used at the internet layer and the port at the transport layer. This post looks at what each of them points to, and what to check when you can’t connect to a server.

IP addresses and ports

An IP address is a number that identifies a computer on a network. IPv4, the version most in use, is written as four numbers between 0 and 255, like 192.168.0.20.

A port is a number that identifies the program receiving a request within one computer. It is between 0 and 65535; a server program picks a port when it starts and waits for requests on it.

Part of the address Points to
192.168.0.20 The computer receiving the request
8080 The program on that computer receiving the request

Nginx, a backend app and Redis can run on the same server because they use different ports, so requests reach the right program without getting mixed up.

Default ports

Commonly used programs have a default port they use when none is specified.

Port Program that uses it by default
22 SSH
80 HTTP
443 HTTPS
3306 MySQL, MariaDB
5432 PostgreSQL
6379 Redis
8080 Spring Boot, Tomcat

A browser uses 80 for an http:// address with no port, and 443 for an https:// address with no port. So https://example.com is the same as https://example.com:443.

Public and private IPs

A public IP is an address that is unique across the whole internet. Internet service providers hand them out, and any computer on the internet can reach that address.

A private IP is an address used only inside an internal network, such as an office or a home. These three ranges are reserved for private IPs.

Range Example
10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255 10.0.0.5
172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255 172.17.0.2 (Docker’s default container range)
192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255 192.168.0.20

Each internal network uses private IPs on its own, so 192.168.0.20 at one company and 192.168.0.20 at another are different computers. That is why a private IP can’t be reached from the internet. How computers on an internal network get out to the internet, and how requests from outside get in to an internal server, are covered in the next post on NAT and port forwarding.

Check your PC’s IP with these commands.

What you see here is the private IP. The public IP the internet sees can only be found by asking an outside service, as with curl ifconfig.me.

localhost and 0.0.0.0

localhost

localhost is the name for the computer running the command itself; its IP is 127.0.0.1. Requests to it don’t leave for the network but go to a program on the same computer.

The address a server listens on

A server program decides not only the port but also which address it accepts requests on. This is called binding.

Bind address Who can connect
127.0.0.1 Only programs on the same computer
0.0.0.0 Every network address of that computer. Other computers can connect too
192.168.0.20 Only requests arriving at that address

Even on the same port 8080, a server bound to 127.0.0.1 can’t be reached from another PC. Defaults differ by program.

Program Default binding To allow other PCs
Vite dev server localhost npm run dev -- --host
Spring Boot All addresses Nothing to change
Redis 127.0.0.1 (per its config file) Change bind, set a password
Docker -p 8080:80 0.0.0.0 -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 keeps it to the same PC

0.0.0.0 is a bind value meaning “accept on every address”. It isn’t an address to type into a browser; to connect, use localhost or the computer’s IP.

localhost inside containers

In terms of networking, a container behaves like a small computer inside the server. Each container has its own IP and its own 127.0.0.1. So where localhost points depends on where you use it.

Where localhost is used What it points to
The server’s terminal The server itself
Inside the app container The app container itself
Inside the api container The api container itself

Even on the same server, connecting to localhost:8000 from the app container looks for app’s own port 8000, not api’s. No program is listening there, so the connection is refused. Reach another container in one of these two ways.

Method Address used from app Condition
Through the server 192.168.0.20:9000 api runs with -p 9000:8000
Docker network api:8000 Both containers on the same Docker network. The container name becomes the address

For the same reason, a program inside a container binds to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1. -p sends requests arriving at the server to the container’s IP (172.18.0.3), so a program bound only to 127.0.0.1 inside the container never receives them. Who can connect from outside the container is decided by the server address in front of -p: -p 9000:8000 lets other PCs connect, and -p 127.0.0.1:9000:8000 only allows connections from that server.

This is also why writing the backend address as localhost in an Nginx container’s config doesn’t connect. The actual setup for both methods is in Connecting containers in the Nginx post.

Port conflicts

One port on one address can be used by only one program. Start another program on a port already in use, and it fails to start and exits.

Find the program using that port and stop it, or change the new program’s port.

Checking open ports

Which program is listening on which address and port on a server is checked with ss.

Option Meaning
-t tcp. TCP connections only
-l listening. Only ports waiting for requests
-n numeric. Ports as numbers instead of names like http
-p process. The program using the port. Programs of other accounts only show with sudo

The Local Address:Port column is the bind address and port. In this output, Nginx (80) and SSH (22) are on 0.0.0.0, so other PCs can connect; Redis (6379) is on 127.0.0.1, so only this server can.

Firewalls

Even when a server is listening on 0.0.0.0, a firewall blocking requests to that port means no one can connect. A firewall is a program that allows or blocks incoming and outgoing connections by rules you set.

Where Examples
On the server ufw and firewalld on Linux, Windows Firewall
Network equipment A company firewall, a home router
Cloud Rules in front of the server, such as AWS security groups

Check whether another PC can reach the port with these commands.

Order for checking connection errors

The message you get when a connection fails narrows down the cause.

Message Meaning Likely causes
Connection refused Reached the server computer, but no program is listening on that port The program is down, the port number is wrong, it is bound to 127.0.0.1
Connection timed out No response came back A firewall is blocking, the IP is wrong, a private IP from another network was used

Check from the server side outward.

  1. On the server, use ss -tlnp to see whether a program is listening on the port.
  2. Check that the bind address isn’t 127.0.0.1.
  3. On the server, check that curl localhost:8080 gets a response. If it does, the program is fine.
  4. From another PC, check with nc or Test-NetConnection whether the port can be reached. If not, look at the firewall or the network.

Command summary

Task Command
Check your PC’s IP ipconfig (Windows), ip addr (Linux)
Check the public IP curl ifconfig.me
Check open ports and programs sudo ss -tlnp
Find the program using a port ss -tlnp | grep :8080, netstat -ano | findstr :8080
Check the response on the server curl localhost:8080
Check port reachability from another PC nc -zv IP port, Test-NetConnection IP -Port port

item.title: Network layers
item.description: Covers the TCP/IP four layers and OSI seven layers for looking at network communication in layers, and how data is wrapped as it passes through them.
item.content:encoded:
When you type an address into the browser, the request goes through several steps before it reaches the server. This post looks at how those steps are split into layers and what each layer does. It is the groundwork for placing IP addresses, ports, NAT and HTTPS, covered in the following posts, in their layers.

Why split into layers

Network communication needs several jobs done together. The format of what is exchanged has to be agreed, the receiving program has to be found, a route to the receiving computer has to be found, and the data has to be sent as a physical signal. Splitting these jobs into layers lets each layer do only its own job and hand delivery to the layer directly below it.

With the layers separated, changing one layer leaves the others as they are. Switch a laptop from a wired LAN to Wi-Fi and the HTTP request the browser sends does not change, because the actual transmission is the job of the bottom layer.

TCP/IP four layers

The structure the internet actually uses is the TCP/IP four layers. From the top down:

Layer What it does Address it uses Examples
Application The format of what programs exchange URL, domain HTTP, DNS, SSH
Transport Finds the receiving program and decides how to deliver Port TCP, UDP
Internet Finds the receiving computer and the route to it IP address IP
Network access Actually transmits within the same network MAC address Ethernet, Wi-Fi

On the sending side, data goes down from the application layer to the network access layer; on the receiving side it goes back up. A router in between only handles up to the internet layer, where the receiving computer is found.

Network access layer

Actually transmits data between devices on the same network. The address used here is the MAC address, a unique number on every network card or Wi-Fi chip, written like a4:5e:60:12:34:56.

A MAC address is only used within one network. When data crosses into another network, the router sends it on with the MAC address of the next segment.

Internet layer

Delivers data by looking at the receiving computer’s IP address. When the destination is on another network, routers look at the destination IP and pass the data to the next router, over and over, until it arrives. Public and private IPs and NAT belong to this layer.

Transport layer

Hands data that reached the computer to the receiving program by its port number. The delivery method is either TCP or UDP.

TCP UDP
Connection Sets up a connection before sending Sends right away, with no connection
Delivery check Confirms receipt and resends anything missing No check
Order Delivers in the order sent No order guarantee
Used for HTTP (1.1, 2), SSH, database connections DNS lookups, video calls, games

TCP delivers everything in order, at the cost of the time the checks take. UDP is faster, at the cost of possibly losing some data. Video calls use UDP because showing the next frame matters more than re-receiving a late one. HTTP/3 uses QUIC, which builds its own delivery checks and ordering on top of UDP.

Application layer

Defines the format of what programs exchange. A browser and a web server use HTTP, a terminal and a server use SSH, and turning a domain into an IP uses DNS.

TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the set of rules that encrypts the data being exchanged and checks, with a certificate, that the server you connected to is genuine. Sending HTTP wrapped in TLS is HTTPS. TLS works between the application layer and the transport layer: it encrypts the HTTP content and then sends it over TCP. When counting the TCP/IP four layers, it is usually described as part of the application layer.

OSI seven layers

The OSI seven layers is a reference model that splits the same ground into seven finer steps. The internet itself runs on the TCP/IP structure, but OSI layer numbers are often used when describing devices and technologies.

OSI layer Number TCP/IP layer
Application 7 Application
Presentation 6 Application
Session 5 Application
Transport 4 Transport
Network 3 Internet
Data link 2 Network access
Physical 1 Network access

The numbers in device names like “L4 load balancer”, “L7 load balancer” and “L3 switch” are these. L4 means it decides by looking up to the IP and port; L7 means it looks as far as the HTTP path and headers.

Encapsulation

When data is sent, it goes down from the upper layers to the lower ones, and each layer adds a header with its own information in front. This is called encapsulation. The receiver does the reverse, removing the headers one by one from the bottom layer up.

Here is what each layer adds when an internal PC (192.168.0.31) requests https://example.com/api/users.

Layer What it adds Name of the data at this step
Application An HTTP request such as GET /api/users, Host: example.com Message
Transport Source port 51000, destination port 443 Segment
Internet Source IP 192.168.0.31, destination IP 198.51.100.10 Packet
Network access Source MAC, MAC of the next device Frame

With HTTPS, the HTTP request part sits behind the TCP header encrypted by TLS. Devices along the way can see the IP and port, but not the request path or content.

Devices along the way only read up to the header of the layer they handle. A router looks at the IP header to choose the next route and does not read the HTTP content above it. A reverse proxy like Nginx, on the other hand, reads the HTTP headers and path to decide where to send the request.

Layers that devices and tools work at

Device or tool What it looks at Layer
Switch MAC address 2
Router IP address 3
Router NAT, port forwarding, Docker -p IP address, port 3, 4
Ordinary firewall IP address, port 3, 4
L4 load balancer IP address, port 4
Nginx reverse proxy, L7 load balancer HTTP path, headers 7
Web application firewall (WAF) HTTP request content 7

When a connection fails, checking from the lower layers up narrows down the cause.

Command Layer it checks What success tells you
ping 192.168.0.20 Internet Data reaches that IP
nc -zv 192.168.0.20 8080 Transport A program is listening on that port
curl http://192.168.0.20:8080/ Application The server answers over HTTP

Firewalls often block ping, so a failed ping does not mean the layers above it fail too. In that case, check again with nc or curl.

item.title: Access tokens and refresh tokens
item.description: Why token-based login splits access tokens from refresh tokens, and where each token is kept and how it is refreshed.
item.content:encoded:
The previous post said that with tokens the server stores nothing, so it can’t invalidate a token it has already issued. This post looks at splitting tokens into access tokens and refresh tokens to reduce that problem, and at where to keep the two tokens and how to refresh them.

The examples assume the page and the API are on the same origin. If they’re on different origins, the settings in the cookies post are also needed.

Why two tokens

A single token lifetime is hard to get right.

Lifetime Upside Problem
Long (e.g. 14 days) Users don’t have to log in again A leaked token can be used by someone else for 14 days
Short (e.g. 30 minutes) A leaked token is useless after 30 minutes Users have to log in again every 30 minutes

So two tokens with different jobs are used.

Access token Refresh token
Job Proves the user on API requests Gets a new access token
Sent to Every API request Only the refresh request (/auth/refresh)
Lifetime Short (e.g. 15–30 minutes) Long (e.g. 1–2 weeks)
Format Usually a JWT A JWT or a long random string
Stored on the server No Yes (database, Redis)
  • The access token travels with every request, so it has many chances to leak. In exchange its lifetime is short, so a leak does damage only briefly.
  • The refresh token is sent only when refreshing, so it has few chances to leak. Because the server stores it, deleting it on the server makes it unusable immediately.

Since the refresh token is stored on the server, this approach adds some of the benefits of sessions to tokens. Requests don’t need a store lookup (access token), while logout is handled on the server (refresh token).

There’s no single right lifetime. A shorter access token means less damage if it leaks but more refresh requests; a longer refresh token means fewer logins but a longer window in which a leaked token can be used.

Sending tokens

There are two ways to send a token to the server.

Authorization header Cookie
Who adds it The page code, on every request The browser, automatically
Does the page code need to hold the token Yes No (with HttpOnly it can’t even read it)
Is it attached to requests sent by other sites No It can be (blocked with SameSite)

As in the previous post, how the token is sent is chosen separately from whether you use sessions or tokens. A JWT can be sent in a cookie too.

Where to store tokens

On login you receive an access token and a refresh token, and you have to decide where in the browser to keep each. The options are localStorage, browser memory and an HttpOnly cookie.

Keeping something in browser memory means not writing it to browser storage, only to a JavaScript variable in the code running in the open tab. It isn’t on the server. When the page reloads or the tab closes, the code starts over and the value is gone.

Where Is it memory
A module variable (let accessToken), React state, a Zustand store Memory
A Zustand store using persist Not memory. persist saves the value to localStorage

Where a token is kept determines how dangerous an attack becomes.

XSS and CSRF

A token becomes dangerous in two ways. Both are attacks from the cookies post.

The token is stolen (XSS): If an attacker hides a script in a post’s content, the script runs in the browser of any user who opens that post. The script reads the token and sends it to the attacker’s server.

The attacker then calls the API from their own computer with that token, acting as the user until the token expires.

The token is used without the user knowing (CSRF): The browser adds cookies to requests automatically. If the user opens the attacker’s site while logged in, that site can make a request to our server, and the user’s cookie goes with it. The attacker never learns the token’s value, but uses the token through the user’s browser.

Comparing storage locations

Location Stolen (XSS) Used without the user knowing (CSRF) After a reload
localStorage Scripts can read it Not sent automatically, so not applicable Kept
Memory The variable is hard to reach Not applicable Gone
HttpOnly cookie Scripts can’t read it Sent automatically, so it must be blocked with SameSite and so on Kept

Each has trade-offs, so the two tokens go in different places.

Where each token goes

The refresh token goes in an HttpOnly cookie. It’s valid for a long time, say 14 days, so if it’s stolen, new access tokens can be obtained for that whole period. So it goes in an HttpOnly cookie that scripts can’t read, and cookie attributes block it from being used without the user knowing.

  • SameSite=Strict: the cookie isn’t sent with requests that start from another site.
  • Path=/auth: the cookie is sent only with refresh and logout requests, not with other API requests.

The access token goes in memory or localStorage. The page code has to put it in the Authorization header of every request, so it has to be somewhere the code can read. In exchange it’s short-lived, say 30 minutes, so a stolen one is useless 30 minutes later.

Memory localStorage
Stealing it Hard Easy
Reload, new tab Gone, so it has to be fetched again with a refresh request Still there, used right away

No storage location stops XSS itself. While a script is running, it can send requests as the user even without reading the token. XSS is prevented by never inserting user input into HTML as is, and by limiting which scripts may run with a CSP (Content Security Policy) header.

CORS settings

The attacker’s site can also make the user’s browser call our server’s /auth/refresh. The attacker’s site and our server are different sites, so a SameSite=Strict cookie isn’t sent. Even with a setting that lets the cookie go along, the browser doesn’t show the response holding the new access token to the attacker’s site, because reading a response from another origin requires the server’s permission through CORS.

This protection holds only while the server allows CORS narrowly. If it allows every origin and also sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, the attacker’s site can read the response and take the new access token.

The CORS setting depends on where the page and the API live.

Page and API CORS setting
Same origin (Nginx or a dev server proxy forwards /api and /auth) Not needed. Leave it unset
Different origins (app.example.com and api.example.com) Allow only the page’s address

With different origins, list the origins to allow. In Spring:

With Spring Security, this setting is applied with http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()).

An example setup

The examples in this post put everything above together like this.

Item Setup
Refresh token HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/auth cookie
Access token Browser memory (a JavaScript variable). Fetched again from /auth/refresh after a reload
CORS Unset on the same origin; on different origins, allow only the page’s address
XSS Never insert user input into HTML as is, and set a CSP header

The access token also works in localStorage. That saves a refresh request on every reload, but if XSS happens, the token can be taken and used for the rest of its lifetime.

This is one way of setting things up where the page code handles the access token itself; there are others.

Setup What the browser holds Characteristics
This post’s setup Access token (memory), refresh token (HttpOnly cookie) The page code handles the access token
Both tokens in HttpOnly cookies Two cookies The page code never touches a token. Every API request needs CSRF protection
BFF (Backend for Frontend) One session cookie A server dedicated to the page keeps the tokens and calls the API on its behalf. No token in the browser, but one more server
Sessions A session ID cookie No tokens. Covered in the previous post

Refreshing tokens

When the access token expires, the API returns 401. On that 401, the page code gets a new access token with the refresh token and sends the failed request again.

If the refresh request fails too, the refresh token has also expired, so the user is sent to the login page.

Issuing and refreshing in Spring

  • The access token goes in the response body; the refresh token goes in Set-Cookie.
  • @CookieValue reads a value from the request’s cookies. The refresh token is HttpOnly, so the page code never knows its value; the browser sends it as a cookie.
